records.title: Grampian Against Data Centres
records.bodyText:
Water infrastructure is becoming a real concern as data centers expand. When Cheyenne, Wyoming traced a rare bacterium to wastewater from a contractor working on Meta's facility, the city revoked discharge privileges and took its reclaimed-water system offline for months of cleaning and investigation.
The contamination didn't reach residential drinking water, but it exposed something larger. As these massive facilities multiply, communities are starting to ask harder questions about cooling water, wastewater management, and what gets dumped into local systems after construction.
It's a reminder that industrial growth has real consequences for water quality and availability. What happens upstream affects everyone downstream.

Herald letters
I DON’T know if Chris Allan (Letters, October 3) discussing the threat to golden eagles from wind turbines intended to be frivolous. It certainly came across as such. I’d go as far as describing it as facetious.
The use of phrases such as “a rabbit taking a leak” and “sliced and diced” certainly suggest he isn’t taking the matter seriously.
Whilst a golden eagle’s eyesight may well be good enough to spot a rabbit two miles away, the tip of a rotor blade, which might be travelling at anything from 120 to 180mph, would be much more difficult to see and avoid.
The golden eagle is a rare and precious part of our natural heritage and should be cherished as such. The death of even one bird is one too many. Everything possibly should be done to mitigate risk.
David Clark, Tarbolton.

Kilbraur Wind Farm
A twenty-seven turbine wind farm within the valley of the Scottarie Burn, 7 miles (11 km) west northwest of Brora in E Sutherland, Kilbraur Wind Farm was built in two phases 2006-08 and 2009-11. 
The first phase comprised 19 German-built Nordex turbines which, together with their support towers, were delivered by sea to Invergordon and then moved to site by road. Each is 70m (230 feet) in height, with blades which are 90m (295 feet) in diameter, giving a total height to blade tip of 115m (377 feet). 
The first phase also necessitated the construction of 4½ miles (7.5 km) of access road, some sections of which were built on bed-rock while others float on top of deep peat formations. 
A second phase, costing £29 million, brought a further eight turbines mounted on 80m (262 feet) towers, but with the same blade dimensions, giving a total height to blade tip of 125m (410 feet). All of the installed turbines produce 2.5 MW of electricity, giving the site a total peak generation capacity of 67.5 MW.
The project was developed by RDC Scotland and West Coast Energy Ltd., with work undertaken by contractors Tulloch Civil Engineering Ltd. and R.J. McLeod Ltd. 
The wind farm is owned and operated by Kilbraur Wind Energy Ltd., which is a subsidiary of Falck Renewables (now Nadara). Kilbraur Wind Energy Co-operative was established in 2008 to allow local people to invest in the project and a community trust fund also distributes grants to support local projects.— at Kilbraur.

Rosyth Dockyard Power Station (Commissioned 1912)
Power Station (Building No 333), Rosyth Dockyard, A Category B Listed Building in Rosyth, Fife
Summary Category B
Group Category Details 100000019
Date Added 19/12/2006
Local Authority Fife
Planning Authority Fife
Burgh Dunfermline
NGR NT 09970 82330
Coordinates 309970, 682330
Construction by Easton Gibb and Son Ltd of Westminster for Royal Navy, 1910-15. 3-storey and attic/single storey with false attic and 2-storey and attic/single storey and attic and 2-storey; also with concealed basement; overall L-plan power station; comprising 3-storey and attic/single storey and attic main block.  
Building interior consists of steel-framed roof-trusses to main block, which is largely open to roof. Brown glazed tiled dado to ground floor; white glazed bricks to arched basement. Formerly contained steam turbines (since removed). Retains original crane (inscribed 'Marshall Fleming & Co, Motherwell' and dated '1914').
The Rosyth Dockyard, Basin and the Pumping Station, the @power station was the earliest building to be completed on the site (it is shown nearing completion in a photograph dated 1912). One of the key buildings at the dockyard, it would have supplied power to the whole complex, including to any ships stationed there. It remains one of the dockyard's landmarks, despite having lost its original industrial chimney, which also served as a clocktower. It is amongst the earliest non-public electric power stations remaining in Scotland. Rosyth dockyard is the largest facility used by the Royal Navy outside southern England. It constitutes the only newlybuilt naval dockyard in the UK since the Napoleonic era.
The decision to construct a major naval base facing Germany was announced in 1903. Subsequently the Admiralty purchased 285 acres of foreshore and 1184 acres of inland around Rosyth. Operations did not begin however until March 1909, with Messrs Easton Gibb and Son Ltd of Westminster appointed as contractors. It was intended as a support and heavy repair base for warships of the Grand Fleet.
At the outbreak of the First World War very little of the work had been completed. Work was underway on the main basin and the tidal basin to the east had been constructed (although its entrance was obstructed by a clay dam); the generating station and pumping station had been built but were only in the process of being equipped. More manpower was sent to speed up the construction process and the dockyard was officially opened by George V in June 1915. The main basin however was not entirely completed and flooded to full depth until September. Between March 1916 and the Armistice, 78 capital ships (dreadnoughts, superdreadnoughts and battle cruisers), 82 light cruisers and 37 small craft were docked and refitted at Rosyth. The yard's value soon became apparent, when a number of damaged warships were towed in for repair following an engagement with the German High Seas Fleet off Jutland in June 1916.
The design and building of the electricity generating station became an early priority. As soon as the plant was commissioned, its power could be used both during the construction period and later for Naval operational use.
The provision of Naval repair facilities were to be of the highest standard. The workshops were to be comprehensive and able to undertake all types of ship repair and reconstruction following damage of warships in battle. The workshops would provide the best mechanical cutting and turning lathes available and these had to be supplied by reliable electric power. To service these excellent facilities there was the need to build a correspondingly excellent generating station. The contract specification for the generating plant was as follows:
Five separate engines will be provided, each rated 250 horse-power, each with its own dynamo giving an output rating of 175 Kw at 550 volts. When working at full power a total horse-power of 1,250 would ɓprovide 875 Kw of electricity.
With this multiple power plant it would be possible to maintain supply should any unit fail or be under maintenance.The combined output from this central generating plant was considered generous when first proposed. However, soon other generating stations in the United Kingdom would soon outstrip the total electric capacity of Rosyth.
The decision to use coke as the primary source of power resulted in the engine fuel being water gas. This does not give the highest calorific value of the alternatives, but it is easy to produce and relatively cheap. This is a gas made up of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, C+ H₂0 CO + H2
The five driving engines were to be powered using this fuel by a method known as the Suction Gas process. The gas was obtained by passing steam over incandescent coke. When ignited in the cylinders the exhaust gases were carbon dioxide and water. The reason for the name of suction gas arose from the engine cylinders directly sucking the gas from the adjoining coke firebox. The engine ran on the four stroke principle conceived in 1876, ironically by the German inventor Nicolaus August Otto. The actual units installed were listed as "National, twin cylinder, suction gas engines, running on the Otto principle". The ignition sparks were created by low tension magnetos. How these big engines were started is a mystery. The cranking mechanism would not have been manual and was probably driven by a small separate engine, using a belt lying round a clutched pulley.
During the construction of the generating station, a fire broke out on 11th June 1910. The cause was in the timber shuttering and a large fire resulted. It would be some weeks before replacement parts to the metal coke stoves were available.
The dockyard was run down after the Armistice and closed to naval use between 1928 and 1935. However during this period at least one dry dock was used for breaking up ships salvaged by Cox and Danks after scuttling in Scapa Flow. It came back into full operation during the Second World War. After the war it was kept operational to support forces deployed to counter the Northern and Baltic fleets of the Soviet Navy. In the late 1960's it was designated a major refitting base for the Polaris (strategic ballistic missile) nuclear submarine fleet.
This is an extract from a Dockyard history which may be of interest:
1955 -Rosyth Dockyard stopped generating its own electricity supply in the Generating Station. After that date, high voltage AC was imported from the National Grid and transformed down to suit the various levels of supply required around the Yard and aboard ship (ie 440V/415V 3 phase 50 & 60 Hz, 115V single phase 50 & 60 Hz and Direct Current). The frequency of the shore supply remained at National Grid level of 50 Hz and was changed to 60 Hz by synchronising machinery for supply to ships. Ships under refit did not use their own generators to produce electricity and this was supplied from the Dockyard and known as the shore supply..
Following the end of the Cold War, operational ships and the majority of uniformed personnel were withdrawn between 1993 and 1996. The dockyard was transferred to commercial management in 1987 and sold to Babcock in 1997 (with limited guarantee of naval contracts). It continues in use as a working dockyard on both naval and commercial contracts.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it's still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That's part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency - such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances - have played an important role too.

Coast Guard & Sinking of F/V Mistress January 1, 2019 & MP 4 Video
The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) is legally mandated to investigate the sinking of the F/V Mistress. Under 46 U.S.C. § 6301 and 46 CFR Part 4, the Coast Guard has a strict statutory requirement to investigate any reportable "marine casualty" occurring on the navigable waters of the United States
Because the January 1, 2019 sinking of the 52-foot commercial fishing vessel resulted in both the total loss of the boat and the loss of life, it automatically met the legal criteria for a Serious Marine Incident (SMI).
While the initial mandate was technically satisfied, a major shift occurred in September 2026. The nonprofit group Green Oceans located the wreckage 92 feet underwater—just 50 feet from Turbine 1 of the Block Island Wind Farm—and discovered what are believed to be human remains
While the law mandates that the Coast Guard conduct an investigation, it leaves the decision to reopen a closed case to agency discretion. Maritime advocates and the families of the victims are actively arguing that the discovery of new forensic evidence and potential human remains legally obligates the Coast Guard to reopen the file, recover the remains for DNA testing, and thoroughly re-examine how the nearby wind turbines impacted the initial search-and-rescue radar and flight operations

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Three-quarters of people in Scotland say offshore wind farms should only be built where they do not harm nature , according to a new poll.
The polling, commissioned by RSPB, found that there was strong support for offshore wind within Scotland, but only alongside strong protections for nature.
Almost eight in 10 people (79%) said they were more likely to support offshore wind farms away from important wildlife sites. Three in five people said that they thought [Berwick Bank](https://www.heraldscotland.com/.../26222117.berwick.../...), an offshore wind farm off the east coast of Scotland, should only go ahead if its impacts are significantly reduced.
Aedan Smith, head of policy and advocacy for RSPB Scotland, said: "These results show people across Scotland support renewable energy, but not at the expense of our most important wildlife.   You can read the full story here https://archive.ph/fBXjq

records.bodyText:
You may have seen the news....the Glen Earrach Pumped Storage Hydro (PSH) scheme is to face no objection from the Highland Council.
Following some debate at the Highland Council South Planning Applications Committee meeting today, councillors voted 6-6 when it came to deciding whether or not to raise an objection to the scheme.
Our local councillors for the Aird and Loch Ness Ward were also split, taking opposing sides in the debate. Councillor David Fraser raised a motion to object, whereas Councillor Chris Ballance put forward an amendment to raise no objection, but proposed a further two planning conditions.
The casting vote fell to committee chairman Councillor Paul Oldham (Nairn and Cawdor, SNP) who chose to raise no objection to the plans and it was given the green light to proceed. 
To help understand the opposing positions of our councillors (and the views expressed by others), we recommend you watch the meeting and following debate: https://highland.public-i.tv/core/portal/home
Equally, should you have any questions, you may wish to initially raise these with the relevant councillor(s) participating in the meeting. Contacts can be found at: https://www.highland.gov.uk/councillors
The scheme still requires the approval of the Energy Consents Unit. If approved, no works can currently commence until applications for the grid connection and the required Dochfour weir upgrades have also been approved.
There is still much to do, and we will reconvene tomorrow, with more analysis, insights and updates - so advance apologies for more FB posts!
